I'm gonna interview some gamedevs and would like to crowdsource some questions to add to my own.

edit: Thank you all for the input! It will all flow into the podcast.
You want to join the industry. What would you ask a gamedev?
Is it really all Bacon and Coding? Or are there a lot of meetings and crappy business stuff involved too? -Programming Student

Depends on your company, team, and producer. The farther down the hierarchy you are, the less meetings you're subjected to, usually. The higher up the pecking order, and I often wonder how they get anything done with all the meetings they have.

Some producers want the entire team to be involved, so there will be weekly team meetings, which are actually useful if they stay on track. Keeping a team focused and involved lets ideas be heard. Some producers will hold daily meetings, and that's where I feel like my time is being wasted. But, to each their own.

"How specialized does one need to be to get into game AI programming?"

"Are devs forced to use certain APIs or can the team decide before getting down and dirty?"

"Do I have to sell my soul to gaming journalism to make it?"

"How much time do you guys invest into Easter Eggs?"

"Why do you make vidya?"

"Do you play video games?"

"What do you think is the role of mathematics in your games/in the development process?"

"Can you cook?"

"How much exchange is there between the programmers and the storyboard/game designers?"

"How did you land your job?"

"Be honest with me here, do you love what you do? Don't weasel out. Give me a yes or no and some justification."

To just name a few questions I'd ask. Very basic stuff
"Do I have to sell my soul to gaming journalism to make it?" This.

I've been in the industry over a dozen years, so...

"How specialized does one need to be to get into game AI programming?"

Depends on the size of the studio or game. The larger the group you work in, the more specialized each person is expected to be. Smaller groups require their members to wear more hats.

"Are devs forced to use certain APIs or can the team decide before getting down and dirty?"

Not as certain about this one, but usually the decisions on software are made at the higher paygrades... if there's money involved.

"Do I have to sell my soul to gaming journalism to make it?"

Not at all. I know precisely one game journalist, and I only met him through community theatre. We've talked about video games considerably less than computers and acting and Star Wars. Unless you're your own publisher it's probably not a problem. There's usually a relationship between journalists and publishers, not journalists and developers.

"How much time do you guys invest into Easter Eggs?"

Not much. Easter eggs are generally jokes that occasionally get implemented near the very end. Most of the process of making a game is just getting the $%&#ing thing to work right and hunting down bugs. Occasionally a team or an individual gets enough free cycles to pursue their own interests, and that's where easter eggs generally come about. If they survive management, they end up in the game.

"Why do you make vidya?"

Personally, I went to school for animation with a desire to go into film & video. But all my friends & family are in the Chicagoland area, and Chicago sucks for film. There's a number of video game companies around, though, so... I animate.

"Do you play video games?"

Yes, I do, but a surprising number of folks in the industry don't. I worked with one guy who didn't own a television or computer at home. Currently I play TF2, Darkest Dungeon, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, and FTL.

"What do you think is the role of mathematics in your games/in the development process?"

Without math, you guess, and guessing is an awful way to solve problems. Math isn't required, but I use it quite a lot. In addition to solving problems, I write scripts and tools for art, which uses at least a little math.

"Can you cook?"

Yes, and I enjoy cooking.

"How much exchange is there between the programmers and the storyboard/game designers?"

Programmers and storyboard artists don't have much conversation between them. I'm not certain about designer-programmer conversation, but I imagine it's quite a bit. Regardless, designers are usually quite happy to talk. And talk. And talk.

"How did you land your job?"

I was working at Best Buy, which is an awful experience, and looked up "motion graphics" in the phonebook. Found a local company there, went in and applied. Was brought in under a free internship which lasted two weeks, then got hired on part-time after I proved myself competent. After I graduated college, I was bumped up to full-time.

"Be honest with me here, do you love what you do? Don't weasel out. Give me a yes or no and some justification."

Usually yes.

Usually my job has me animating cool stuff, working on cool projects with cool people. I bounce from topic to topic (animate a guy jumping onto a moving vehicle. OK, now animate a dog running) and from talent to talent (animate, make a script, set up this hardware) which keeps things interesting. And in the end, I can show people a cool game or video I worked on and have them know I don't play video games all day or some other nonsense perpetuated by Grandma's Boy.

But sometimes things aren't so cool. Sometimes I'll be asked to redo an animation a dozen times because a Designer didn't do their job right and design the move. Or they attempted to describe what they want using sound effects. (Seriously. I've gotten "It needs more shwoomp!" as feedback.) Sometimes an animation is tedious. Animating cloth is boring after two weeks straight.

And other times, the project itself doesn't interest me. It's hard to be creative about boring stuff. Or sometimes you work with people you just want to strangle, but that's any job.

But overall, I'm happy to do what I do. I hear my friends from high school talk about their jobs as accountants or insurance adjusters and my brain goes numb with boredom.
